blocks.content: 1. Why Consistency Models Exist

On a single machine, every read trivially returns the latest write, there is only ever one copy of the data. The moment a system replicates data across multiple nodes, to handle more traffic, to survive a node failing, or to serve users near their own region, a new question appears for every single read: which copy is this actually hitting, and how far behind might it be?
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272784652-650494568.png
blocks.alt: Replication is what turns 'read the data' into 'read which possibly-stale copy of the data'

blocks.content: Consistency models answer that question precisely. They define exactly what a client is guaranteed to see when it reads, and that guarantee is what everything built on top of the system can safely assume. Pick too strong a model and you pay for coordination you did not need; pick too weak a model and your application has to defend against surprises it was not built to handle.
2. The Spectrum: Strongest to Weakest
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272787458-890013666.png
blocks.alt: Consistency models form a spectrum, each one relaxing a specific guarantee the previous one made

blocks.content: Every model below gives up a little more than the one before it, in exchange for lower latency, higher availability, or both. None of them is simply "better", each is the right answer for a different kind of data, this is exactly the kind of choice the CAP theorem and PACELC frame at a higher level, these models are what that choice actually looks like in the code.
3. Strong Consistency (Linearizability)

The strongest model. After a write completes, every subsequent read from any node returns that new value, immediately. The system behaves as if there were only ever a single copy of the data, even though many replicas actually exist underneath.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026159-893395036.png
blocks.alt: Once a write's linearization point passes, no client anywhere can observe an older value again

blocks.content: Formally: every operation appears to take effect at a single instant, its linearization point. If write W finishes before read R begins in real time, R must observe W's result, with no exceptions.

blocks.title: Cost
blocks.content: Every write must be acknowledged by all, or a strict quorum, of replicas before confirming to the client. Latency scales with the slowest participating replica, and an unreachable node means waiting or failing the write outright, this is the CP end of the CAP tradeoff made concrete.

Used for: financial ledgers, distributed locks, leader election, anywhere a stale read is a correctness bug rather than a minor inconvenience. Google Spanner, etcd, and ZooKeeper's linearizable reads are built for this.
4. Sequential Consistency

Slightly weaker than linearizability. All operations appear to happen in some single, agreed-upon order, and every client sees that same order, but the order is not required to match real wall-clock time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272790938-419921025.png
blocks.alt: Every client agrees x = 1 happened before x = 2, even if they each found out at a different moment

blocks.content: Concretely: a system writes x = 1, then later x = 2. Every client that reads both values sees x = 1 before x = 2, but one client might learn about both writes sooner than another, delay is allowed, disagreement about the order is not.

Used in: distributed shared memory systems and multi-processor architectures. Less common as a database's advertised default, but it appears frequently as the ordering guarantee underneath message queues and replication logs.
5. Causal Consistency

Weaker still, but smarter about what actually needs ordering. Operations that are causally related, one depends on or was triggered by the other, must be seen in that same order by every node. Operations with no causal relationship can appear in any order without violating anything.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272792634-488252789.png
blocks.alt: A reply must always appear after the message it replies to, but an unrelated message can land anywhere

blocks.content: A causal relationship means: if operation A happens, and operation B is created knowing about A, using A's result, or coming from the same session, every node must show A before B. In the diagram, Bob's lunch reply causally depends on Alice's original message, so no one should ever see the reply before the question. Carol's unrelated comment about the weather has no such dependency, so it can be seen in any order relative to the lunch conversation.

Used in: MongoDB's causal-consistency sessions, Facebook's social graph, collaborative editing tools. A strong fit for social and collaborative applications where conversational order matters but paying for a full global order everywhere would be needlessly expensive.
6. Eventual Consistency

The weakest common model, and the most scalable. If no new writes arrive, every replica is guaranteed to eventually converge on the same value, but during the convergence window, different nodes can return different, older answers to the exact same read.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396026161-541362203.png
blocks.alt: Replicas are allowed to disagree temporarily, the only promise is that they converge once writes stop arriving

blocks.content: There is no bound on exactly when convergence happens, only a guarantee that it eventually will, assuming the system keeps propagating updates and no new conflicting writes keep arriving.
Conflict Resolution in Eventual Consistency
When two nodes accept different writes for the same key during a partition, the system needs a rule for reconciling them once the partition heals.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272795993-748606213.png
blocks.alt: Three common strategies for the same underlying problem: two replicas that disagree

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","How It Resolves a Conflict","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Last-Write-Wins","Keeps whichever write has the later timestamp, discards the other","Simple, but silently loses one of the two writes"],["Vector Clocks","Detects that a real conflict occurred and surfaces both versions to the application","No silent data loss, but the application must know how to merge"],["CRDTs","Data structures mathematically designed so any merge order converges to the same result","No conflict resolution logic needed at all, but only certain data shapes support it"]]}
Used in: Cassandra, DynamoDB, CouchDB, DNS, anywhere staying available matters more than always returning the single freshest value.

A concrete vector-clock example: two shopping cart replicas both start knowing about version [A:1, B:1]. Replica A accepts an add-to-cart write and advances to [A:2, B:1]; during the same partition, replica B independently accepts a different add-to-cart write and advances to [A:1, B:2]. Neither vector is a strict ancestor of the other, so the system flags this as a genuine concurrent conflict rather than silently picking one, and Amazon's original Dynamo design specifically merges both carts' items together in this exact situation rather than discarding either customer's addition.
7. Read-Your-Writes Consistency

A practical middle ground, and one of the two "session guarantees" alongside monotonic reads. After a client writes something, that same client is guaranteed to read its own write back on any subsequent read. Other clients may still see stale data, but the writer never sees an older version of what they themselves just wrote.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272797788-738439300.png
blocks.alt: The writer always sees their own update; a different client may still be reading a replica that has not caught up yet

blocks.content: How it is implemented: route all of a client's reads to the same replica it wrote to, sticky sessions, or attach a version token to the response so the system can pick a replica that is at least that far along before answering that client's next read.

Used in: most databases with session-level consistency, PostgreSQL read replicas configured with session affinity, DynamoDB's strongly-consistent read option scoped to the writer while other readers use eventually-consistent reads.
8. Monotonic Read Consistency

Once a client has read a particular value, every later read by that same client is guaranteed to return that value or a newer one, never an older one. Reads only move forward in time for a given client, they never appear to go backward.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272799450-960794445.png
blocks.alt: Reading x = 7 and then later x = 3 is exactly the kind of disconcerting, backward-looking read this guarantee forbids

blocks.content: Without this guarantee, a client could read x = 5 from one replica, then read x = 3 from a different, less caught-up replica on its very next request, an experience that looks like the data spontaneously reverted.

How it is implemented: track a version token, timestamp or sequence number, per client, and only serve that client's reads from a replica that is at least as up to date as the last version it already observed.
9. Categorizing All the Models at a Glance
blocks.text: 9. Categorizing All the Models at a Glance

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272801246-861068080.png
blocks.alt: Every model covered so far falls cleanly into one of four buckets, from strictest to loosest

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bucket","Models","What It Guarantees"],"rows":[["Strong","Linearizability","Every read anywhere sees the latest write, immediately"],["Ordered","Sequential, Causal","Everyone agrees on an order, though not necessarily real-time delivery"],["Session","Read-Your-Writes, Monotonic Reads","Guarantees scoped to one client's own session, not the whole system"],["Weak","Eventual","Replicas converge eventually, with no bound on exactly when"]]}
10. Choosing the Right Model
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272802872-915593596.png
blocks.alt: The real question is always what a stale read actually costs for this specific piece of data

blocks.content: There is no universally best model, the right one depends entirely on what a given piece of data can tolerate: wrong data, no data, or a brief delay before the freshest data shows up.

Real systems rarely pick one consistency model for the entire application. A payment platform commonly uses strong consistency for account balances, read-your-writes for a user's own transaction history so they immediately see their own payment, and eventual consistency for a fraud-analytics dashboard that can tolerate being a few minutes behind.
11. Tunable Consistency: Choosing Per Operation, Not Per System
blocks.text: 11. Tunable Consistency: Choosing Per Operation, Not Per System

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272804582-921461805.png
blocks.alt: A single cluster commonly runs several consistency models at once, one per table or one per operation

blocks.content: Many real databases let this choice be made per query rather than fixed once for the entire cluster. Cassandra lets a client request consistency level ONE for a fast, loosely-consistent read and QUORUM or ALL for a strongly-consistent one, on the very same table. DynamoDB exposes an explicit strongly-consistent-read flag alongside its eventually-consistent default. This mirrors the quorum mechanics covered in the CAP Theorem topic: the W and R values chosen per operation are, in effect, choosing a consistency model per operation.

The example below models three of the guarantees above directly: a tiny replicated store where a strongly-consistent read always waits for every replica to agree, an eventually-consistent read can return a stale value from a lagging replica, and a read-your-writes read is correctly routed back to the replica the same client actually wrote to.
12. Real-World Systems and Their Default Consistency Model
blocks.text: 12. Real-World Systems and Their Default Consistency Model

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272806210-757078856.png
blocks.alt: Well-known systems each ship with a deliberate default, and most let you override it per query

blocks.content: {"headers":["System","Default Model","Notes"],"rows":[["Google Spanner","Strong (linearizable)","Uses synchronized atomic clocks (TrueTime) to make global strong consistency practical"],["etcd / ZooKeeper","Strong (linearizable)","Built specifically for coordination tasks where a stale read is unacceptable"],["MongoDB","Causal (with sessions)","Causal consistency is opt-in per session; default reads are eventually consistent otherwise"],["Cassandra","Tunable, defaults to eventual","Per-query consistency level from ONE up to ALL, see section 11"],["DynamoDB","Eventual, with a strong-read option","Strongly-consistent reads cost roughly double the read capacity of eventual ones"],["DNS","Eventual","Propagation delay after a change is the direct, everyday experience of eventual consistency"]]}

Notice the pattern: systems built specifically for coordination default to strong consistency because that is the entire point of using them, while systems built for massive scale default to eventual consistency and treat strong reads as an explicit, opt-in, more expensive request.
13. Strong Consistency's Real Cost: Multi-Region Latency
blocks.text: 13. Strong Consistency's Real Cost: Multi-Region Latency

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272807852-486277263.png
blocks.alt: Strong consistency across continents is bounded by the speed of light, not just by software efficiency

blocks.content: Strong consistency within a single data center is cheap, network round trips there are measured in fractions of a millisecond. Strong consistency across regions on different continents is a fundamentally different cost: a round trip between, for example, a US and an Asia-Pacific region can add well over one hundred milliseconds, and a linearizable write needs to wait for that round trip before confirming.

This is exactly why globally distributed strong-consistency systems like Spanner invest so heavily in specialized infrastructure, precisely synchronized clocks, purpose-built network paths, rather than simply running an ordinary quorum write across distant regions and accepting the latency. For most applications, the more common and far cheaper pattern is the one from the CAP Theorem topic's multi-region section: strong consistency inside a region, eventual consistency across regions.
14. A Common Mistake: Assuming One Model Must Cover Everything
blocks.text: 14. A Common Mistake: Assuming One Model Must Cover Everything

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785272809850-797059589.png
blocks.alt: Different pieces of data inside the same application routinely need different consistency guarantees

blocks.content: A frequent design mistake is picking a single consistency model, usually whichever the primary database defaults to, and applying it uniformly to every table and every feature. In reality, a shopping cart, an account balance, and a product recommendation list rarely have the same tolerance for staleness, and forcing all three through one model either wastes latency on data that never needed strong consistency, or risks real correctness bugs on data that did.

The fix, as section 11 covers, is to make the choice per operation or per data type deliberately, exactly the same mix-and-match discipline the CAP Theorem topic recommends for choosing between CP and AP.
Worked Example 1: A Collaborative Document Editor
blocks.text: Worked Example 1: A Collaborative Document Editor

blocks.content: A collaborative document editor needs causal consistency for the edit history, so that a comment reply always appears after the comment it responds to for every viewer, regardless of which server handled which edit. It needs read-your-writes for the editing user specifically, so a person who just typed a paragraph never sees their own cursor jump backward to an older version of the page.

Meanwhile the document's own view count, shown quietly in a corner of the screen, is eventually consistent, a count that is a few seconds behind causes no confusion and costs nothing extra to serve at scale. Three different guarantees, deliberately chosen per feature, inside the exact same application.
Worked Example 2: A Banking App

A bank's core ledger, the actual account balance used to approve or reject a withdrawal, runs strongly consistent, backed by a system like Spanner. A stale balance here could let an account go overdrawn or double-spend the same funds across two ATMs, a correctness bug with real financial consequences.

The same app's transaction notification feed, the push alert telling a customer "$40 spent at Coffee Shop", is read-your-writes for that customer's own device but eventually consistent for anything else, a notification arriving two seconds late is a minor annoyance, not a financial risk. The monthly spending-summary dashboard, aggregated from potentially millions of transactions, is fully eventually consistent, computed on a delay from analytics pipelines that would be needlessly expensive to keep perfectly real-time.
Common Mistakes

["Defaulting to whatever consistency level the database ships with, instead of deliberately choosing one per data type","Confusing eventual consistency with 'usually consistent' and skipping conflict-resolution logic entirely, then being surprised when two replicas genuinely disagree","Assuming causal consistency requires a full global order, when it only needs to order operations that are actually causally related","Forgetting that read-your-writes is a per-client guarantee, not a system-wide one, other clients can still see stale data during the same window"]
items: Defaulting to whatever consistency level the database ships with, instead of deliberately choosing one per data type
Confusing eventual consistency with 'usually consistent' and skipping conflict-resolution logic entirely, then being surprised when two replicas genuinely disagree
Assuming causal consistency requires a full global order, when it only needs to order operations that are actually causally related
Forgetting that read-your-writes is a per-client guarantee, not a system-wide one, other clients can still see stale data during the same window

blocks.content: Practice

For a food delivery app, decide which consistency model fits each of the following, and justify the choice: the restaurant's live order queue position, the customer's own order history, the restaurant's star rating shown to browsing customers, and the payment charge itself.

Then explain, in your own words, the difference between sequential consistency and causal consistency, and give one example of two operations that would need ordering under sequential consistency but not under causal consistency.

As a third exercise, pick two of the last-write-wins, vector-clock, and CRDT conflict resolution strategies from section 6, and describe a specific scenario, beyond the shopping cart example, where one of your two choices would handle a conflict noticeably better than the other.
Key Takeaways

Consistency models exist because replication turns a simple read into a question of which possibly-stale copy is answering it. They form a spectrum from strong, linearizable consistency down to eventual consistency, with sequential, causal, and the two session guarantees, read-your-writes and monotonic reads, sitting in between, each relaxing a specific promise in exchange for lower latency or higher availability.

No single model is correct for an entire application. Real systems choose per data type, often per operation, using tunable consistency levels that mirror the quorum mechanics from the CAP Theorem topic. The next topic, Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation, moves from these qualitative tradeoffs to the concrete numbers used to size a system before any of these decisions get implemented.
